en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Determining Sin and Merit, Volume One.

Master Ming Shou... [text missing] ...should quickly deliver one's own life... [text missing] ... (Note: The provided source text contains significant lacunae and illegible characters, indicated here by ellipses and placeholders.
The translation reflects the extant portions of the title and the thematic content of such sutras.)
It is the mandate of Heaven.
It is the essence of Heaven and the life-force of man. It is longevity.
It is beneficial to burn incense and light lamps as offerings.
One should offer three five-zhang long banners of various colors for the gift of longevity,
writing one's own name upon each banner.
The reason it is five *zhang* high is that because humans violate the five precepts, they incur five offenses;
therefore, it is five *zhang* high.
The reason there are three [images] is to rescue those in the three evil realms; it is because the Three Honored Ones come forth to deliver beings from the triple world.
Those whose transgressions are great are difficult to rescue.
Prepare food and drink of seven flavors to provide for the assembly of noble ones, and possess the three dharma-robes;
observe the fast and precepts for seven days,
and three times each day reproach yourself for the transgressions committed by your body, speech, and mind.
Taking refuge in the Triple Gem and upholding the names of the eight Buddhas,
one shall receive the offerings of burning incense, scattering flowers, and lighting lamps;
for a full seven days, one shall bestow blessings and plant roots of virtue.
With a mind of loving-kindness, one nurtures those whose aspirations are impoverished.
If one gives to a pure practitioner of the Way,
one will immediately gain an increase in lifespan and eliminate the sins of past lives.
Those who have lost their property due to being struck by calamities from local officials, water,
or fire should likewise observe the fast and precepts, reproach themselves for their fundamental transgressions,
and swiftly establish meritorious deeds to extinguish those misfortunes.
First, if one reaches the third [recitation] after completing the extinction [of the transgression],
the offense will be immediately eliminated.
Furthermore, one should follow the teacher’s instructions and must not harbor doubts regarding the teacher.
The Master has delved deeply into the treasury of the sutras;
one must not measure the Master with the ordinary mind that dwells on birth and death.
To serve as a teacher for others is a most difficult task.
The teacher bears a heavy responsibility and acts as a guarantor;
he must not follow the disciples' fluctuations of status, causing them to lose the Way and the Dharma.
This will bring no benefit in the present life and lead to entry into hell after death.
In this way, one permits people to commit transgressions,
lacks great compassion,
and fails to show people the Great Illumination.
If one does not save another's life,
or causes another to lose their lifespan while practicing virtue,
these are all the fault of the teacher.
The teacher instructed his disciple,
yet the disciple did not follow the teacher’s instruction, nor did he believe or accept it.
Later, when the disciple died, he entered hell.
Although he wished to cite his teacher as a divine witness,
his teacher’s teachings were not followed;
that person had committed the offenses himself and was entirely uninvolved in the teacher's affairs.
The Bodhisattva Huìfǎ addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there shall be five ages of turmoil.
The first is the turmoil of the people."
Second is the disorder of the royal way;
third is the disorder of the ghosts and spirits;
fourth is the disorder of the people’s hearts filled with anxiety and fear.
Fifth is the corruption of the Dharma.
At such a time, when the fourfold assembly of disciples relies upon the Dharma,
how can they attain deliverance from the world?
The Buddha told Huifa:
"At that time, the disciples of the fourfold assembly will all have weak resolve and feeble precepts."
They do not guard the gates of the sense faculties, allowing their six consciousnesses to run wild;
their minds are distracted and disordered as they study heterodox scriptures,
while their speech is verbose and their appetites are insatiable.
Those with defiled minds and impoverished conduct compete for hollow fame;
those of similar appearance follow one another, and those of similar wealth associate with one another.
Tranquil and steady in conduct,
one’s mind does not dwell on the mouth or engage in miscellaneous speech.
When the multitude of desires delude the mind, the many bears follow of their own accord.
When one's words and deeds are at variance,
one shall go to the Palace of Mount Tai after death; there,
one's merits and transgressions are finalized.
Intending to repent for themselves, they were unwilling to listen; thus,
those entering the three miserable realms are many,
while those attaining human status are few.
The Dharma-preacher Hui-fa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"At that time, the fourfold assembly of disciples was distressed, defiled, and turbid."
Obscured by turbidity and lacking clarity of hearing,
how can one who is within [this state] act as a teacher to save others?
How could such a person grasp the intention of the Buddha?
Thus they fail to grasp the Buddha's intent and cannot summon even the deities of the lower realms;
they are perpetually unable to deliver themselves.
"How can one deliver others?
The Buddha told Huifa:
"At that time, there were many sentient beings who sought the Buddha."
They are like the myriad stars;
those who have attained the Way are few.
Those who can uphold the precepts and guard the Way are like the sun and the moon.
Those who refute my doctrine are my disciples, and not others.
Because they engage in eating, drinking, walking, rising, and dressing,
they are no different from worldly people; thus,
the devas find no pleasure [in them] and do not descend to submit [to their teachings].
Calamities and pestilences spread abroad;
water and grass were not in harmony, the five grains were not harvested,
and the common people suffered from hunger and exhaustion.
Water and grain do not nourish him;
he finds no flavor in his food;
his face lacks its natural luster.
The people suffer much from illness;
their internal organs are in disharmony,
and various malevolent spirits take advantage of this decline and sickness to afflict them.
Consequently, they proceeded to perform divinations and exorcisms for various spirits;
cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, wine, and various delicacies were offered as food,
which the *liang* and *wang* ghosts and spirits then consumed as they moved in and out at will.
He transforms his physical form to appear like a corpse,
falsely assuming a name,
and because of the patient's own exhaustion and decline, he manifests as small.
At times they may even kill people;
they exhaust the dwellings of those seeking tranquility, and whatever they turn toward brings misfortune.
Such individuals never realize on their own that their conduct violates the Buddha’s teachings, claiming instead that they have already served the Buddha.
Furthermore, when their food declines,
they do not realize it is caused by their own transgressions;
instead of reproaching themselves, they resent the heavenly deities.
Ceasing to perform virtuous deeds and offering prayers for sheep at sacrifices,
they suddenly lose their lives and enter hell;
whereas those who observe the precepts and practice according to the Dharma [attain liberation].
They do not sink or float with the world;
they maintain an upright body, practice the Dharma, wear the monastic robes, and have few desires.
They are able to practice the four immeasurable minds and compassionately regard all people throughout the ten directions.
These are all great bodhisattvas.
Although they exist in an age of decline and turmoil, such as this,
true persons continue to teach and transform beings everywhere.
Because there are such people, the myriad subjects are each able to hasten to them to receive their holy transformation;
they distance themselves from the conduct that leads to hell and seek the path to transcend the world.
Such a person who maintains this practice is then able to foresee good and ill fortune.
The celestial deity said to him: "You must not speak with such arrogance, saying, 'The celestial deity has come to speak with me.
Those who have attained the Way shall all experience illness; know that this is caused by the retribution of past transgressions."
"You should extinguish it yourself.
One who fulfills my Dharma is my disciple;
one who destroys my Dharma is also my disciple."
"It is truly not another.
The monk Huifa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Regarding the people of future generations and all the disciples..."
When conduct violates ritual and precepts, celestial calamities arise;
sentient beings suffer misfortune—
how can we bear such pain?
"Because the teacher was not clear in his instructions and failed to cultivate the precepts,
it happened thus because he did not act according to the Buddha's words.
The Buddha told Huifa:
It is exactly as you have said.
If there is a wise teacher who instructs and admonishes men and women,
proclaiming the Buddha’s true Dharma to teach and admonish the people.
The practitioners were numerous;
the multitude collectively reviled him,
and some even harbored hatred and jealousy toward him.
Now that the Buddha-dharma has declined and the true teaching has become obscured and stifled,
there is no longer any long-term benefit;
this is the great Māra within the Buddha-dharma who causes the Dharma to be destroyed.
The Dharma Master Huìfǎ addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Furthermore, in the final age, if the teachers and the Dharma are not clear,
may one cease and not study the Buddha-dharma?"
The Buddha told Huìfǎ:
"A human body is difficult to obtain;
the Way of the Sūtras is difficult to hear."
One should seek out a wise teacher from afar and receive the five precepts from them;
one should serve them with compassion and filial piety, providing them with food, clothing, and other necessities.
Provide medical treatment for the sick.
Ensure that incense, flowers, and lamps are never lacking.
Observe the six fast days in accordance with these instructions; you shall thereby obtain merit, attain the Way, and realize the fruits of enlightenment.
The Dharma Master Hui said to the Buddha:
"One who wishes to receive the dharma of the precepts must enter into the purity of the sūtras and vinaya,
and seek out a clear and virtuous teacher who is well-versed in understanding the Buddha’s teachings."
Why is this so? A teacher is like a father.
If a father serves his office diligently and attains high distinction, [his son shall likewise be honored].
The high ministers and officials of the rank of two thousand shi,
as well as the kinsmen of their various clans and all their relatives both within and without the court,
received no small measure of glory. As for the households and the minor local officials of the commanderies and counties, none dared to harass or approach them.
If even the transgressions of one's own children are all extinguished by it,
how much more so those of ordinary people?
The Buddha-dharma is likewise.
The Master’s precepts are pure, so he shall swiftly attain Buddhahood;
the disciples receive his radiance, whereby their heavy [karmic burdens] are removed and lightened.
Transcending the three evil realms through these precepts, they shall be delivered across immeasurable [suffering].
It is also like the crown prince of a king, who ascends to the highest position and is not equal to the common people or minor officials.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"It is so, it is so. It is exactly as you have said, without any difference.
The Bodhisattva Prajñādharma addressed the Buddha, saying:
If there are good men or good women who are afflicted by illness or misfortune,
or who have legal matters involving the local authorities;
Pursued by past karmic offenses,
they wish to repent their transgressions and seek deliverance,
or they wish to seek merit and retribution in future lives.
One should offer flowers, incense, wealth, treasures, and clothing as alms.
If one uses silk brocades, banners, and canopies to make offerings to the Buddha in pursuit of merit,
would it not be even more so for a Daoist who maintains the precepts?
"To please you as you wish," [he said].
The Buddha replied,
"I shall now question you in turn."
Answer as you please.
I am like a great king who has several sons.
"The princes and those below them are all unworthy.
Only this humble youth is intelligent, compassionate, and benevolent.
After the King’s hundredth year has passed, to whom should the kingdom be entrusted?"
Huidfa replied, "I shall give it to my younger son,
for the responsibility entrusted to him is great."
"One who is an unworthy son cannot shoulder the heavy responsibilities of a state.
The Buddha said,
"The King of the Kāruṣas possessed immeasurable wealth."
The family had several dozen sons.
The eldest and the youngest were both unworthy,
while the middle son was clever, wise, compassionate, benevolent, and filial.
"To whom should the inner doors of the treasury be entrusted?
Wisdom-Dharma replied to the Buddha,
"The unworthy son destroys the doors."
One must not place trust in them;
they will surely take their parents' wealth and treasures and spend them on unworthy things,
to no benefit for their parents.
The Buddha said,
"So it is, so it is. Within my Dharma, it is likewise."
If a son or daughter of good family wishes to give offerings of banners, silks, flower canopies, clothing, precious gems, and wealth,
their transgressions shall become purified.
For a Daoist who maintains the precepts and enters the Vinaya, providing for them most urgently results in the fulfillment of merit and virtue;
they shall thus fall upon the ground of the Three Honored Ones.
However, for one who does not maintain the precepts, merit and virtue are not thereby accomplished.
Or they may consume food and drink, or desire to use it for their own pleasure;
their bodies become unworthy as they eat and drink at improper times,
never mindful of the donor's household.
They personally set aside their own status as husband, wife,
and children to practice giving to practitioners of the Way for the sake of the Buddha-dharma;
yet these practitioners do not merely receive the offerings of the faithful out of gratitude for the Buddha's grace alone.
Though one may obtain wealth and profit in this life,
if one does not consider sin and merit and fails to use them at the proper time,
and furthermore disregards the divine spirits, one shall not attain great riches.
"It is not that they lack merit.
The Bodhisattva Huifa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there are good sons or good daughters..."
If one is afflicted by a ghost,
and a śramaṇa is summoned to recite the scriptures,
is this done because it accords with one's own inclinations, or is it required for the sake of purity?
The Buddha said,
"One must be even more pure and clean;
only then can one subdue and eliminate all demons and malevolent spirits."
One must also do so with a sincere heart.
At times, the Buddha suffered from a headache and called Śāriputra, saying, "Read a sutra for me."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The original sūtra was heard and received from the Buddha;
it is something Śāriputra does not know."
"It does not equal the wisdom of even a single hair of the Buddha.
How can you, on the contrary, preach the sutras for the Buddha?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I wish to hear the sutra.
My body is in extreme agony.
Śāriputra, come quickly and preach the sutra for me."
If, after my passing from this world,
my disciples lose their protection and those who have not yet attained the Way all fall within the realm of Māra.
They shall likewise be preyed upon by Māra.
It is because I do not wish for my disciples to mutually slight, despise, or treat with contempt the sutras and the Dharma that I have done so.
*Jue zui fu jing*, Volume One.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Resolving Sin and Merit, Volume II.

The Bodhisattva Hui-fa addressed the Buddha, saying: "If good sons or good daughters receive the five precepts of the Buddha, or receive the ten precepts, or become śramaṇas and receive the two hundred and fifty precepts, and desire..."
Seeking the path to transcend the world, one may fail to attain one’s desires due to the influence of past transgressions.
Or, having practiced evil in previous lives, resentment and hatred may arise from all sides;
or one may suffer a short lifespan, or fall victim to untimely death amidst the chaos of a degenerate age.
Afflicted by the disease of a hungry ghost, his life hung by a thread.
With a sincere heart, he took refuge and sought salvation.
As he was pursued by the retribution of past offenses, how could he extinguish them?
The Buddha said:
"What you have asked is most excellent.
It is for the sake of seeking to eliminate all calamities and misfortunes, to extinguish past karmic offenses, to quell the disasters of kalpas, and to eradicate all afflictions."
He reveals the Great Illumination to all people;
he brings peace to everyone so that none fail to receive it.
You shall obtain blessings and attain liberation.
Reflect upon this well and keep it in your heart,
so as to extensively deliver all beings. If there are those who uphold the Buddha’s precepts and Dharma, [you should protect them].
If one seeks the path to transcend the world but is pursued by past karmic offenses,
or if one's life span is short and should be extended through salvation,
and if there is an auspicious sign such as a bird crying out the name of a person;
This concludes the calculation of names.
It is appropriate to provide offerings of food and drink of ten flavors to the assembly of noble ones;
to prepare three dharma robes, five-colored banners and canopies fifteen feet in length, and to offer lamps to the Buddha.
Offer seven lamps to the Queen Mother of the Upper Ghosts;
offer one lamp each to the Four Heavenly Kings;
and offer one lamp to Śakra, Lord of the Gods.
Burn incense, scatter flowers, and observe the precepts of fasting.
At the three periods of the day, repent and reproach oneself for one's original transgressions.
Take seven kinds of incense and place them within oil.
Make good use of sesame oil.
Use new cloth for the pillars.
Use fresh, clean, and excellent soil.
Use clean eating vessels and keep them new.
Provide fresh water for washing the hands and ensure that all utensils are kept bright and clean.
Remove pungent scents and keep them within the heart; never let them pass through the mouth.
Remaining in the ancestral temple, they practiced with diligence day and night for seven days and seven nights.
The celestial offices and ghostly officials recorded these great merits;
by virtue of these merits, their transgressions were expiated, and this was immediately reported to Śakra-devānām-indra.
Their lifespan increases and their years are augmented; their transgressions are eliminated and their calamities are extinguished, while blessings arise. They shall immediately obtain as desired:
those of superior wealth shall give alms to a thousand people, and those of middling wealth shall give alms to five hundred people.
The lower grade consists of two hundred people who give alms;
the banners are also of three grades,
with the superior grade being five zhang in length.
The medium grade is three zhang;
the inferior grade is one zhang five chi.
Dharma robes are likewise of three grades.
The superior consists of seven sets;
the middling, five sets;
and the inferior, three sets.
The Dharma Master Hui said to the Buddha:
"If there are impoverished people whose food and clothing do not continue,"
Pursued by a multitude of transgressions,
one ought to practice giving through almsgiving (*dāna*).
If one is unable to obtain ceremonial banners, colored silks, or Dharma robes, what should the method be?
The Buddha said:
"The poor are also of three grades.
Those of the lowest grade of poverty shall make seven banners, five chi in length, for the sake of giving to seven persons."
Those of middling poverty should provide one banner and one set of Dharma robes;
those who are extremely impoverished should offer incense, flowers, and lamps according to their means,
while maintaining the precepts with all their heart and soul.
After fifteen days, one also attains liberation according to whatever is required by the mind.
Then the Bodhisattva Huidharma addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How can one know the weight of the World-Honored One’s auspicious responses?
The Buddha said,
"Both the monastic and the lay have their own auspicious responses."
When the Bodhisattva was first born, there were thirty-two auspicious omens.
Throughout the ten stages of the Bodhisattva’s path, there are ten dream-omens that serve as proof.
When ordinary people are born, there are no such auspicious omens.
At the time of his impending death, there were auspicious omens;
specifically, there were thirty-two such auspicious omens,
as well as ten kinds of evil dreams that served as auspicious signs.
What are the thirty-two auspicious omens?
First, large birds wailed mournfully;
second, small birds entered human dwellings.
Third, seeing white light;
fourth, a dog looking into a well;
fifth, a dog lying upon a person’s bed and bedding.
Sixth, a dog shed tears toward a person.
Seventh, a dog howled.
Eighth, a beam broke.
Ninth, the eaves are exposed.
Tenth, the rafters are white.
Eleventh, the cooking pots and pans are red.
Twelfth, the bottom of the cauldron is white.
Thirteenth, the spout is white.
Fourteenth, one sees ghosts holding weapons and staffs entering a person's house.
Fifteenth, worms appeared in his food.
Sixteenth, when he raised his voice, it sounded like the crowing of a cock.
Seventeenth, his dog died and departed, or else the dog of another person died and came to him.
Eighteenth, the reflection of one's face does not appear in a mirror.
Nineteenth, the human body gradually becomes emaciated and wasted away.
Twentieth, one suddenly becomes excessively fat and well-favored.
Twenty-first: the human body easily undergoes its usual transformations.
Twenty-second: within the house, there is great clamor at dawn.
Twenty-third: ghosts call out the names of people.
Twenty-fourth: smoke and fire emerge from the hearth in reverse.
Twenty-fifth: mounds of earth are raised at the sides of the gateways.
Twenty-sixth: straw is piled up around the gateways, wells, and hearths.
Twenty-seventh: being lifted up into a window.
Twenty-eighth: a steamer rising from atop a cauldron.
Twenty-ninth: one’s own clothing and cap cutting themselves.
30. Wild insects cry out.
31. Wild insects enter human dwellings.
32. One drinks and commits suicide.
These are the thirty-two auspicious omens.
As for the ten kinds of dreams:
the first is dreaming of entering a prison.
Second, dreaming of being bound by an official;
third, dreaming that all dark spirits follow one;
fourth, dreaming of departing while riding in a carriage.
Fifth, he dreams of falling into a great body of water but not emerging.
Sixth, he dreams of falling into a well but not emerging.
Seventh, he dreams of his house overturning and collapsing to the ground.
Eighth, dreaming that doors fall to the ground;
ninth, dreaming of being buried by a wall or falling into a beam-pit;
tenth, dreaming of being burned by fire.
These are the ten dreams;
all are ominous omens,
yet they can still be remedied.
There are only other omens that are so numerous and immeasurable that those who cannot be saved are not recorded.
If there are minor signs of impending loss of property,
one should instruct them to quickly bring forth their wealth and swiftly perform meritorious acts of giving.
If this person’s merit from past lives has been exhausted and misfortune arises to conflict with others,
they should now diligently cultivate the roots of virtue to assist their physical spirit.
If merit is produced, their body will then benefit.
If one encounters calamities such as water, fire, or legal proceedings with government officials, these are all the result of karmic offenses from past lives.
One should eliminate them through merit and virtue.
If the merit of this person’s past lives is exhausted, their person will then encounter misfortune.
"One whose body is not benefited should cultivate merit and virtue, and thus their body will be benefited.
The monk Hui-fa said to the Buddha,
"Please explain the method for benefiting the body."
The Buddha told Huifa:
"One who has awakened to the fact that there is neither benefit nor peer [in worldly things] should further observe the fasts and precepts and further cultivate all manner of goodness."
With a heart of loving-kindness and filial piety,
further disseminate the seeds of grace and virtue;
you should diligently practice giving.
Burn incense, light lamps, and scatter flowers as offerings;
reproach one's own faults and do not dwell on the evils of others;
when seeing the transgressions of others, regard them as if hearing the taboo names of one's parents.
One should simply guard the actions of body, speech, and mind;
if these three karmas are constantly virtuous,
calamities will no longer arise.
Repenting one's transgressions immediately eliminates sin;
ten thousand evils will never again come.
Wherever one dwells, one shall find companionship.
The Bodhisattva Huifa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a good man or a good woman has committed offenses in past lives and has not yet attained the Way in this present life,"
"How is this to be known?
The Buddha told Hui-fa:
"In a previous life, he borrowed wealth from others and gave it as alms."
If one steals another's wealth,
or plunders another's wealth,
or gives away objects left on the ground as an act of almsgiving;
In this life, although one may obtain great fortune as a human being,
wealth and possessions will not remain long; they pass through one's hands and depart,
or one may encounter enemies and various evils.
He reproaches his master for being robbed by others,
deceived by thieves, and cheated out of money by swindlers.
One should always remain anxious and fearful,
encountering corrupt officials, water, fire, and bandits;
this is because in past lives one took pleasure in killing living beings.
In this life one has a short lifespan;
in past lives one inflicted painful suffering upon others throughout many lifetimes,
and thus in this life one constantly suffers from many ailments.
One receives the retribution for what was sown in previous lives within this present life,
just as one plants grain and harvests its yield,
or plants merit and obtains merit.
Sowing poverty results in poverty:
having failed to practice generosity in previous lives,
one is now destitute in this life.
Due to harsh speech in previous lives,
one fails to attain the supreme flavor of the Buddha-remembrance sutras in this life and frequently encounters misfortunes.
In past lives, they took life according to their capacity;
in this present life, they frequently encounter epidemics.
In past lives, they probed nests and broke eggs.
In this present life, they die in the womb,
or die upon being born on the ground;
in previous lives, they were those who, out of greed for profit, killed living beings by pulling their fur, feathers, or horns.
In this life, one shall become a silkworm;
because in a previous life one burned mountains and marshes,
in this life one repeatedly encounters the perils of water and fire.
In previous lives, they used water to irrigate fox dens, city walls, and thatched huts;
in this present life, they repeatedly encounter floods and die by drowning,
and they contract diseases as a result of their past planting of illness.
Planting the seeds for a short life, one obtains a short life;
planting the seeds for calamity, one obtains calamity; planting the seeds for misfortune, one obtains misfortune.
Planting merit brings merit;
one receives retribution according to what one has planted,
just as planting fruit-bearing trees results in the harvest of fruit.
It never departs from its original seed;
though the body perishes, the calamity remains undecaying,
following one like a shadow follows a person.
"When calamities are about to arrive, there are always auspicious omens.
I wonder, when sins are about to arrive, are there also such omens?
The Buddha told Huifa:
Those whose sins can be averted all experience auspicious omens;
yet there are also those who experience none.

Furthermore, there are instances where birds cry out and dogs howl, where one forgets to see the red light, or where foxes and cats cause disturbances, or where one has evil dreams and feels irritable beyond measure—these cannot be recounted one by one.
If one possesses [merit], one should swiftly establish further merit; at such a time, one should resolve and say:
"The merit now being performed is used to repay past debts."
This shall also serve to eliminate their offenses and cause them to attain boundless merit hereafter.
Now, all the devas and people of the ten directions shall,
by virtue of my merit, attain liberation.
One who can act in this way shall receive protection from all.
If one is about to lose their wealth and possessions due to the karmic offenses of a previous life,
they should immediately leave the household life and cultivate merit with their wealth.
To act thus is a transgression;
it is neither the practice nor the acceptance of the Buddha’s words.
One has not yet ceased from sexual misconduct.
They practiced heterodox paths,
served those *gai* demons,
and offered sacrifices to deities in pursuit of blessings.
They deceive and defraud themselves,
opening the way to the three evil realms;
they turn their backs on the correct path and enter into error.
They abandon blessings to pursue transgressions;
they dwell in decline while serving deities;
they invite calamity and block the path to rectifying their faults.
One detests living while killing one's kin;
one detests pleasure while plundering others;
one detests suffering while practicing benevolence.
One should give alms out of weariness with poverty;
practice respect out of weariness with the base;
and cultivate reflection out of weariness with the ugly.
One who loathes wealth practices stinginess;
one who loathes life takes life;
one who loathes longevity does not arise.
To loathe satiety and discard it;
to loathe former curses;
to loathe security and walk toward peril.
One who loathes danger practices security;
one who loathes security practices goodness;
one who loathes goodness does not practice giving.
One grows weary of death and practices the Path;
by counting the breaths one enters dhyāna, and through the cessation of formations one attains peace.
When the mind ceases, one attains Nirvāṇa.
The sun illuminates the day, and the moon illuminates the night;
meditation illuminates the Path,
and a bright mirror illuminates forms.
Armor and weapons illuminate the army;
meditation illuminates the Way;
a person is defined by being human.
The sun and moon are the essence of heaven;
the Way is the father of the people;
the virtue of the precepts is the mother of the people.
Those who share the same teacher are as brothers;
the kinship of the Way and its Dharma is more profound than that of blood.
Therefore, if a person is loyal, trustworthy, filial, and obedient, they shall remain free from affliction for successive kalpas.
Loyalty, trustworthiness, filial piety, and obedience are what people observe; learning requires single-mindedness, and in every matter one should respond with inner clarity.
A worthy person who exerts diligent effort can attain liberation;
yet if one does not uphold the precepts and the Dharma, allowing the mind to run wild and unrestrained, one cannot escape.
Sins arise like clouds;
the four paths are blocked and the three realms of suffering open wide.
As the roots of sin grow ever greater, the retribution received knows no end.
When the human mind thinks of good, there is an immediate reward of good;
when the mind thinks of evil, there is an immediate retribution of evil;
and when the mind contemplates the Way, one subsequently attains the Way.
The mind is the sovereign of both sin and merit;
it is the child of the Way,
and it is also the mother of all things.
It is also the great niraya.
Virtue and evil, beauty and ugliness, poverty and nobility, wealth and status, wisdom and folly, suffering and joy—
all arise from the mind.
What one does with sovereign mastery, one receives as its own retribution.
A wise person who perceives the truth calculates that the day of birth is not the span of life for the day of death; they truly reflect upon themselves:
"My body will not last long."
One must likewise return to death;
recorded by one's sins and merits, one lacks autonomy.
It is better to rectify the mind, stabilize the intent, direct the single mind toward the Buddha, and serve an enlightened teacher.
They diligently practice the four means of attraction— generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and vigor— as well as single-mindedness and wisdom;
they bestow gifts, act with kindness, benefit others, and seek the common good.
Furthermore, one should practice the four immeasurable minds:
first, loving all sentient beings as a mother loves her child;
second, feeling compassion for the world, desiring to deliver them from falling into [suffering].
Third, with a mind focused on the three liberations, one is always joyful.
Fourth, one protects all beings so that they do not fall into transgression;
one is personally capable of doing so.
Furthermore, if one regrets [one's own faults] and instead finds joy only in reproaching others,
one will ultimately remain far from the evil realms;
upon death, one will attain rebirth in heaven.
While sitting, he called out, and [the deity] arrived standing; the five desires were before him.
Not yet having escaped the realm of death, he was merely approaching the path of the Way.
Then, Huidharma addressed the Buddha, saying:
As the World-Honored One has said:
sentient beings are blind and ignorant, unaware of sin and merit;
they follow the movement of persons, pursuing them without ceasing.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family,
out of ignorance in previous lives, has killed their parents, paternal uncles or aunts, or maternal grandparents;
or has killed śramaṇas or practitioners of the Way.
Some kill their sovereign;
some kill their husbands or daughters;
they kill their mothers, brothers, sons, or even their slaves and servants.
He killed his master.
Because he had committed this sin in a previous life, he died and entered hell;
only after incalculable kalpas will his punishment and guilt finally come to an end.
Due to the remaining merit from their previous lives,
they are born as human beings— whether noble or lowly, male or female—
and are born into an evil age.
Perhaps they encounter government officials,
or they fall upon an age ravaged by pestilence and virulent poisons;
pursued by the remnants of their past transgressions, their lives hang by a thread.
"Is the method for saving them the same as that mentioned above?
One must hear their intention.
The Buddha told Huifa:
Your question is most excellent.
You have such a compassionate heart that you seek to deliver and liberate so many.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it, taking it to heart.
"The Buddha shall explain it to you in detail.
The Bodhisattva Prajñādharma, together with the fourfold assembly,
responded, "Yes, yes," and listened with single-minded attention, desiring to hear it with joy and compliance.
The Buddha told Hui-fa:
"What you have now asked is not the same as what was above.
In the former case, the offense was minor."
"What you have now asked constitutes a great sin;
it is the unpardonable crime of the five heinous acts (*pañcānantarya*).
Although one may eventually escape execution and be reborn as a human being,"
One will inevitably encounter death;
or meet with government officials and be imprisoned in a jail;
or contract a grave illness.
Such people as these do not belong to a single category;
they may be honorable or humble, noble or lowly,
and they may either believe in the Way or believe in worldly customs.
Whether they employ the Dharma or do not employ the Dharma,
those who employ the Dharma should all erect stupas and temples,
and offer up whatever cherished objects they possess from their own persons as offerings to the Buddha.
Furthermore, by making offerings of banners, silks, burning lamps, and incense through past acts of charity,
one may strive to overcome peril and prolong the years of life.
Thus, Hui-fa addressed the Buddha, saying:
If, at a time of emergency,
a person resolves their mind and pledges to establish temples and perform various meritorious deeds,
by virtue of having generated that intention and performed such merit, [the result will follow].
He recovered at once. After his recovery,
he regretted not having done so and said,
"The Buddha said..."
When that person resolves their mind with penetrating clarity,
the various celestial venerables, spirits, the Lord of Destiny, and the Lord of Records, receiving the holy intent of the Buddha,
shall, on account of their great merit, immediately erase their name from the register of death and establish it as a name in the register of life.
Descending as far as the hells, he spoke to the hell-guardians, saying:
"The prisoners and sinners such as so-and-so have already performed great meritorious deeds by erecting stupas and temples."
The merit of performing these six rites is such that it deserves reward;
we shall now restore their original lifespans and the like.
All listen as we release the souls and spirits of [Name].
Whether one is imprisoned in a dungeon or suffers from a grave illness where life hangs by a thread,
the messengers of the Celestial Bureau arrive in unending succession, distributing their documents as swiftly as the wind until they have reached everywhere.
The celestial palaces descended and filled the various hells;
because they had established merit through the Buddha-dharma,
the palaces were immediately leveled, and upon hearing the proclamation, the offenders were released and attained liberation.
After he has departed, Māra will again seize him,
causing that person to feel regret, to have mutual regrets, or to feel regret regarding their faith;
furthermore, Māra will cause parents, brothers, wives, children, and maternal relatives to create obstacles for them.
Furthermore, some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas may also create obstacles.
There may be śramaṇas who, relying on the laws, teachings, and precepts, establish meritorious deeds;
yet such persons do not reckon upon the great merit of enduring through long periods and transcending the world.
Seeking only immediate advantages that please the eye,
they act according to their own convenience, resulting in mutual discord and failure to establish the gift.
One should recognize that Māra may manifest as an official,
water, fire, or the loss of wealth; by halting [the practice] because of these,
one fails to establish oneself and brings shame upon the various devas and spirits due to one's own prior transgressions.
"You should know that such a person's life will not endure long, nor shall they complete their natural lifespan.
The Bodhisattva Huidharma addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there are good sons or good daughters..."
"Once you have consented to the marks of a śramaṇa, you may not act contrary to them.
Would it be acceptable for you to seek whatever else you please as a śramaṇa?
The Buddha said:
In the final age, those who honor the Way and uphold the precepts will be few,
while those who treat the Dharma with contempt will be many.
In this world of the five corruptions, it is extremely difficult to cultivate merit, and demonic obstacles will abound.
Those of great merit encounter three difficulties.
What are these three?
First, it is difficult to resolve the intention to become a śramaṇa.
Second is the difficulty of wishing to establish stūpas and monasteries;
third is the difficulty of wishing to perform the boundless great giving of *pāñcavārṣika* (quinquennial festivals).
These are the three difficulties.
Among these three matters, there are many demonic activities.
One must obtain a person who has entered the discipline and maintains the precepts,
and who is capable of subduing demonic activities.
It is thus possible to govern the minds of people so that they incline toward the gateway of the Way and accomplish their merit and virtue.
If those before us have honored the Vinaya and observed the precepts,
this constitutes reliance upon the Buddha’s Vinaya-piṭaka as appropriate for one's individual needs.
One should manifest the virtues of the Buddha to inspire men and women to develop a mind of great merit;
one must not disregard a śramaṇa according to one's own whims.
Even if the person before you does not uphold the laws and regulations, [one should still treat them with respect].
Furthermore, regarding the request for the dharma of those who uphold the precepts,
the monk Huifa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The śramaṇas delight in purity."
Worldly people delight in crowds;
chickens and owls delight in graveyards.
When they flock together or dwell among burial mounds, their inclinations are fundamentally different.
There may be śramaṇas who wish to erect stūpas in secluded places, such as among mountains, fields, or marshes;
or there may be those who wish to extensively deliver men and women, manifest the Buddha’s virtues, and increase the merit of their patrons.
Regarding those who establish stūpas and temples within a great kingdom,
there may be sons or daughters of good family who wish to build a stūpa on their own land.
Or, if one wishes to build a stupa or temple on the grounds of a hermitage for this reason,
desiring to be near it to pay homage morning and evening and to offer incense and flowers;
"If they do not harmonize, what else should be done?
The Buddha said,
"In the age of the final dharma, people will be wealthy and each will compete to erect stupas and monasteries."
They seek only fame and reputation, not long-lasting and great merit.
There are those who invite śramaṇas wishing to perform deeds of long-lasting and great benefit;
yet these householders seek only immediate, minor gains and do not consider the great benefits of the Path.
This is why the Buddha-temple was built;
by enshrining images within the temple,
one causes people to perform prostrations and worship.
One offers incense, lamps, banners, silken streamers, flowers, and canopies as an act of worship and dedication to bring merit to others.
Furthermore, śramaṇas dwelling at the site of practice (maṇḍala) should cultivate diligent conduct to advance on the Path, extinguishing evil and guarding the good.
It is just as one treats grain and manure to obtain seeds;
for this reason, there is the threshing floor.
The threshing floor and the path are two matters that require one another.
If one wishes for many śramaṇas to dwell therein and recite the sūtras for a long time, and if there are many śramaṇas, the merit will be exceedingly great.
As for those who privately build stūpas where no śramaṇas reside, these are intended only for laypeople; they do not yield great wealth, yet it is not that there is no merit.
In the future, at the end of the age, many people will sell merit.
How do they sell merit?
At that time, the people’s parents will establish private temples and shrines.
If their descendants resemble them and are often impoverished to the point of selling their talismans (fútú),
they are selling their own blessings;
furthermore, they burn themselves so that the money for the talismans enters their bodies.
The Dharma Master Huìfǎ addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there sin for one who purchases merit? Or is there not?
If one acts with full knowledge [of the deception], there is sin."
Huidharma said to the Buddha:
"If a buyer repairs and makes offerings [to it],
by what cause would there be an offense?"
The Buddha said:
"If you did not purchase it, by what cause did you incur an offense?
Suppose there is someone who has promised to erect a stūpa."
"Later, it could not be completed on its own.
You wish to purchase it and repair it; would this be permissible? The Buddha said: "It is permissible."
This is improper.
It is like a person who has committed an offense themselves and subsequently commits a grave offense together with another person.
The attendant knows the situation.
How is it said that [the matter] is concluded?
If one is led away by others and their master is so impoverished as to be unable to provide offerings or practice generosity, may such a person receive [the precepts]?
The Buddha said,
"One may receive [the precepts], but one shall not be exempt from the transgression of failing to fulfill the obligations of a master. Hui Fa said:
Whether it be a man or a woman,
if they are imprisoned and confined,
or if they are afflicted by illness and suffering, once they have resolved in their hearts to cultivate merit, [they may proceed].
Later, one must eliminate one's own offenses.
Why would one not eliminate them?
The Buddha said:
Because the remaining karmic retributions from past lives pursue them,
they may suffer from official persecution or illness;
by resolving to cultivate merit, they shall attain liberation.
When one establishes a new shrine for a deity or constructs a temple,
one can extinguish past offenses and ensure that one’s natural lifespan is fully realized;
furthermore, by repairing a stūpa, one immediately attains merit.
"One should not incur offense.
Śāriputra withdrew from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the time of the final dharma age, the minds and intentions of people will be defiled and turbid."
"How does one who has not yet attained the Way know what constitutes merit and what constitutes transgression?
The Buddha said,
"If that transgression is not recent, then one examines its origins."
If one is imprisoned in a jail and according to the law should die,
yet because human affairs do not reach them and their path is cut off, they die of exhaustion;
or if they are ill and medical treatment does not save them.
If one can escape by relying on the power of merit established through the mind and circulating a general amnesty throughout the world,
you should know that such a person committed the five unpardonable offenses in a previous life.
Although one may eventually be born as a human after the punishments of hell have ended,
one will encounter hardships because of the pursuit of minor transgressions;
only through great merit can one attain liberation.
Thus one knows these to be the result of past offenses.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The four classes of disciples may themselves give rise to the thought [of practice] and create the causes for merit, thereby attaining self-salvation."
"How is it that foolish worldlings alone do not receive this great grace?
What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
Those who receive the instructions and admonitions of a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) shall likewise attain deliverance;
those who do not obtain a virtuous friend shall not find salvation.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What kind of merit is obtained by making a new image of the Buddha?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
By making images of the Buddha, one will be upright and handsome in every lifetime;
after death, one will be reborn in heaven, honored by the devas,
and be most upright and handsome among them.
He shall manifest in the form of a Buddha, being honored, noble, and wealthy in every lifetime, such that no one can equal him;
he shall be one of brilliant intelligence and wisdom, a king among the masses,
and a sovereign over a hundred kingdoms.
All shall belong to them.
They will manifest the form of a Buddha and, in every lifetime, will not be born in a borderland;
they will always be born in the central lands within the families of great kings.
One will always receive the highest love and respect from one's parents, brothers, uncles, and elders.
By creating images of the Buddha, one shall not fall into the three miserable realms or the eight difficult conditions in successive lifetimes.
One will constantly encounter the Triple Gem and remain free from illness in every life.
One will not be afflicted or disturbed by ghosts or spirits;
if one seeks to become a śramaṇa, one will attain success.
Ānanda, the merit of creating an image of the Buddha is exceedingly great.
Now I have spoken but briefly;
it can extinguish great sins.
By fashioning images of the Buddha, one’s body shall be golden in color in every successive lifetime.
From each and every pore, various kinds of subtle and wondrous fragrances issued forth.
In every lifetime, he naturally remembered his past lives.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
It must be done together with pure śramaṇas and lay followers who possess deep faith.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
In this way, one should create illustrations of Buddha shrines and depict their forms and images,
causing the fourfold assembly to prostrate and thereby stirring the hearts of people;
the merit of such an act is vast and great.
"One must be a śramaṇa to achieve profound and great merit.
The monk Huìfǎ said to the Buddha,
"If a person has committed the five heinous crimes..."
"Can the merit created by constructing stupas and temples and making images of the Buddha extinguish [negative karma]?
The Buddha said:
The fires of the five heinous crimes cannot be extinguished suddenly.
Upon death, one enters hell and fully undergoes all manner of retributions.
Even when heaven and earth are destroyed and hell itself perishes, [the consequences remain].
From the destruction of the heavens and earth in other hells in other directions,
they are again cast into other hells in other directions to undergo the retribution of their crimes for kalpas of life that cannot be numbered.
In this manner, they shall undergo further suffering for many tens of millions of years.
When their punishment in hell is finished, they shall fall among the animals as lowly slaves for many tens of millions of kalpas.
Only when their transgressions are exhausted will they emerge and obtain birth as a human being.
Those with the merit and fortune of previous lives become noble persons;
those without the merit of previous lives become lowly persons;
and those whose merit is meager become persons of middle station.

Even if one obtains a human birth, being pursued by even slight transgressions, one will not fully enjoy the span of life; there, one will suffer from verbal abuse, imprisonment and confinement, water and fire, thieves and bandits, enemies, distress, and illness.
One should establish stupas and temples and create images of the Buddha;
as for the incantations and hymns of the blue-robed and white-robed Daoists used to exhort and convert others,
this merit shall indeed extinguish them.
Only then can one extinguish residual and minute offenses.
As for the great offenses of those who have not yet turned their bodies [from this life],
one must instead resolve the mind upon the wisdom of emptiness and clearly understand that all things are fundamentally non-existent.
One must enter deeply into the presence of a good teacher to be able to untie the knots of the mind.
If the knots of the mind are untied, one can then eliminate the dharma of heavy offenses.
Only those who speak thus can grasp the intent of the Buddha.
"Only those such as Mañjuśrī are able to untie the knots of delusion in the mind and eliminate the heavy sins of others.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
While the World-Honored One was in the world, Mañjuśrī appeared;
after the World-Honored One entered nirvāṇa, Mañjuśrī departed.
If the people of the world commit the five heinous crimes, they will not receive salvation at all; being mired in depravity and turbidity, they shall not be spared from these great offenses.
"How painful this is!
O God among Gods.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
Do not grieve. Originally there is no such thing as your mind;
the mind is originally non-existent, being merely the mind of sovereign mastery.
After my parinirvāṇa, Mañjuśrī will maintain the four immeasurable minds;
wherever he manifests transformations, he may appear as a national preceptor or a Daoist master,
or as a lay devotee well-versed in the scriptures.
Some become śramaṇas or brahmins,
their minds delighting in dwelling in the unconditioned;
these recluses perceive that their own physical appearance is insufficient.
Within, there is expedient wisdom that is without phenomena, without awakening, and without entities;
it does not know of a pure mind or a clean intention, and so forth.
It saves all beings, yet there is nothing that is not saved.
One should know that such persons are Mañjuśrī appearing in this turbid age,
who maintains purity, guards the Dharma,
and either possesses profound understanding or has deeply entered the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).
If one appears outwardly dull-witted and ignorant yet possesses inwardly noble wisdom,
they may be relied upon and looked up to;
such a person is capable of averting great transgressions.
"True persons such as these exist everywhere.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha,
saying, "In the future, at the time of the final age, how shall one recognize this true man, Mañjuśrī?"
The Buddha said:
"That person maintains the precepts with purity;
his mind is free from hatred and attachment, and he is without sorrow or grief. He clearly understands Kuśinagara."
This sutra is the refuge; this sutra is held in the heart, destroying [afflictions] and enabling the vast salvation of all.
By means of the Dharma of this sutra, it transforms and delivers the people, such that there are none who do not believe and accept it.
You should know that this śramaṇa or brahmin is none other than Mañjuśrī.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the final age, I shall manifest as a layperson;
when those who act contrary to the Dharma appear, I shall manifest as a śramaṇa."
Amidst turmoil, I dwell alone;
in hardship and confinement, I bring my six spirits to rest.
While others are gathered in crowds, I alone remain submerged in stillness.
If the multitude are asleep while I alone am awake;
if the multitude are intoxicated by the six [senses] while I alone am enlightened by the six [knowledges];
if the multitude delight in suffering while I alone delight in liberation.
The multitude practices what is perilous while I alone practice what is secure;
the multitude is occupied with many affairs while I alone am free from action.
The reason for this is as follows:

Because he wishes to act as a leader for all, those who have not yet attained the Way should all practice silent sitting, remain non-active and free from worldly affairs, maintain the purity of the precepts, and possess few desires; thus they may easily attain the Way.
In the final age, I shall serve as the leader for the multitude;
having realized the Buddha’s unsurpassed, true, and correct Great Way,
I shall cause all people to fully understand the prohibitions of the Dharma.
One should purify the study of the dharma-image for seeking the Way that is free from worldly concerns.
I currently have practitioners who have realized it and can cause those who delight in practicing the Way to do so;
these true persons, the Bodhisattvas, are able to teach us the precepts of non-desire and non-action.
When the six sense-faculties come to rest, one spontaneously attains nirvana.
The Buddha told Huifa:

"That which Mañjuśrī performs is for the benefit of all and for the sake of the True Great Dharma; it is to realize the laws and teachings, to maintain pure precepts, and to carefully guard the outward manifestation of dignified deportment."
This shall cause the Dharma to endure for a long time, bringing lasting benefit.

If, in the future final age, there are those who can guard the precepts, dwell in seclusion, remain free from desire and worldly affairs, have few entanglements, do not frequent defiled places, and maintain the purity of both body and mind while upholding the truth—[for them, this shall serve as a lamp].
All these are Mañjuśrī.
You should seek him from afar, serve and make offerings to him, and receive the five precepts from him.
Should you encounter decline, loss, misfortune, illness, emaciation, death, or trouble with the authorities and verbal disputes, [you must do so].

When seeking merit, one should follow their instructions; whatever is to be given, one should comply with their commands. Whatever is obtained through such merit shall serve to eliminate transgressions.
All possessions that emerge will inevitably decline and perish.
The words of a person of virtue will surely reach the divine; can one not follow them with sincere faith?
To believe in them brings great fortune, while to slander them invites calamity and guilt. Yet, the people of this world are difficult to transform and enlighten.
Blinded, they do not recognize True Suchness;
deaf to the five musical notes, words do not enter their ears,
and though taught, they are unwilling to practice.
Birth and death fundamentally arise from ignorance.
The twelve links of dependent origination cause suffering and decay to continue without interruption.
The five realms of existence are like a turning wheel.
Who would be willing to believe and accept these correct words that seem so contrary?
Only those of the lineage of the Heavenly Response can believe and receive them.
One may practice throughout life without diligent effort in goodness, only to feel regret after death.
Furthermore, water cannot be gathered up, and one must personally experience the retribution of one's own merit and demerit.
It is like a person’s form and shadow, which cannot be shifted or exchanged.
By practicing good, one obtains good; by practicing evil, one obtains evil.
In an evil age, one must not commit evil deeds.
An evil person may first prevail but will later suffer defeat;
they may first be fortunate but will later meet with misfortune.
One must not lose the opportunity for goodness in this world.
To lose such goodness is to punish oneself.
Do not dismiss small acts of goodness as being without merit.
Though drops of water are minute, they gradually fill a large vessel;
if small virtues are not accumulated, one cannot perfect the self.
Do not disregard even minor evils, thinking them to be without fault.
A single drop of water is minute, yet gradually it becomes a great vessel;
small evils do not accumulate enough to destroy one's person.
Both good fortune and misfortune, both calamity and blessing, all arise from the mind.
One must not fail to comply with this.
The five precepts are the foundation of humanity;
the ten wholesome actions are the root of merit.
The five precepts are the root of virtue;
the ten wholesome actions are the seeds of heaven.
The Buddha is the father of all beings.
The Sūtra is the mother of all;
those who share the same teacher are brothers, remaining close to one another for kalpas on end;
those who are skilled in the five precepts are the very limbs of that person.
One who possesses the five precepts attains a human body;
if even one precept is lacking, one does not become a human.
Because people do not possess all five precepts, those who are truly human are few.
Those who raise livestock, hunt, or catch birds are many.
This is why there are three evil states of existence.
Furthermore, there are three matters that are evil and cause people to enter the three evil paths.
What are the three things?
First, evil in speech;
second, evil in thought.
The three evil physical actions are evil.
If these six matters are extinguished, one dies as a human being and is not reborn again.
All ordinary people possess these six evils.
Because ordinary people unite their bodies with these six evils, they do not attain the Way.
They descend into the three miserable realms where the retribution of suffering is difficult to endure and immeasurable.
Foolish men seek fame and reputation; they pursue their desires with unrestrained hearts.
Later, their accumulated faults and sins will be as vast as Mount Tai;
though the fleshly eye perceives nothing of this,
they shall subsequently go to the realm of King Yama in the hells.
Without questioning others, one merely examines the events of the time of birth;
the spirit-consciousness naturally maintains its integrity and dares not harbor concealment or deception.
The heavenly deities clearly distinguish good from evil, with not even a hair’s breadth of error.
Because they attend to their roots, they are able to practice the prohibitions and precepts.

Because they do not contravene ritual and instruction, they fulfill their natural term and reach a timely end. Thus, the worthy observe the beginning and the end and dare not allow themselves to be self-indulgent or unrestrained.
The wise delight in the precepts and are unwilling to transgress them.
There are two things in this world that people covet as profit:
one is that which cannot benefit the spirit.
Of these two matters, one is able to benefit both humans and spirits;
the other is official rank, title, salary,
and position— these are merely empty names.
It cannot benefit the spirit;
when the body dies, the spirit departs far away.
It is like a bird’s eggshell discarded on the ground: the chick does not undergo transformation because of the form of the shell.
It is also like this. For example,
when a silkworm emerges from its cocoon by piercing it with its thread and flies away, transforming its appearance and changing its body,
its spirit remains the same.
It is the same with human beings:
when the body becomes the soil, the spirit wanders through the five realms of existence;
the body and the spirit each depart separately.
This is why they do not know one another.
As for the two matters, they are wealth and goods;
wealth and goods can be given for the sake of merit.
Merit can eliminate transgressions;
merit can deliver one from hardships;
merit can rescue one from peril.
Merit eliminates calamities and misfortunes;
merit can lead one to the Way.
Therefore, we know that wealth and goods are superior to noble rank.
Those who are able to employ wealth through the path of the Dharma will find benefit for their spirits;
those who cannot cultivate merit and virtue through the path will not.
This is no different from [losing] one's noble rank.

All these things—high office and generous emoluments, the assembly of ministers and officials, parents, brothers, wife, children, and kinsmen—are loved so deeply that their affection penetrates to the very marrow of the bones. Yet, after death from worldly illness, all of this is lost.
Who would be willing to accept it?
One cannot expend one's life for the sake of rank and position;
one cannot expend one's life for the sake of power and influence.
It is impossible through words to turn back the formless adversary that forcibly detains the spirit and endangers life.
Only by bestowing blessings and practicing virtue can one benefit the spirit’s efficacy, increasing its years and extending its lifespan.
Just as people in the world who possess abundant wealth can seek out their own livelihoods and enjoy them,
it is likewise within my Dharma.
For those in the world whose merit is exhausted and whose transgressions arrive, [they fall].
A wise person is thus able to bestow and establish great merit.
Great merit is achieved only by means of wealth and goods.
Now, as for the act of giving:
In the present world there is a tenfold retribution;
when it is experienced in future lives, there is a retribution of billions-fold,
incalculable and many times more than that.
I have always spoken only of a ten-thousandfold recompense, but that was merely a brief and minimal statement.
Fearing that people might not believe such a small amount,
I have stated it as being more than double its actual measure.
Just as when one plants the seeds of fruit trees for a young child, the subsequent growth of stems, nodes, and fruits becomes incalculable;
so too, the merit of giving yields a tenfold reward in this present life.
Those who direct themselves toward [this practice] shall always receive protection from their companions.
In future lives, they will receive blessings hundreds of billions of times more than can be calculated.
It is like planting a tree that later grows into a great tree; its roots, fibers, trunk, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are beyond counting.
The same applies to the doubling of the transgressions incurred by committing various evils.
When the Buddha spoke these words,
eighty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
Eighty thousand bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind;
sixty thousand śramaṇas realized arhatship;
and eight hundred million devas and humans resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Twenty thousand upāsakas all attained the stage of srotāpanna;
sixty-four thousand ordinary people shaved their heads and became śramaṇas;
and eight thousand people fully received the five precepts.
One hundred and thirty people arose to cultivate merit and eliminate their transgressions;
only three remained, pursued by residual karma, lying sick upon their beds. They resolved to establish merit, and all the sick were cured.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the name of this sutra?
How should it be practiced and upheld?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This is called the *Sūtra on Determining Sin and Merit*.
You should constantly uphold it."
He extensively bestowed this teaching upon all the devas and human beings.
It was for the sake of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others;
for the great assembly of bodhisattvas, the community of bhikṣus, and Ānanda and his peers.
The king, the people, and all others were filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.

The *Buddhabhāṣita-jue-zui-fu-jing* (Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Determination of Sin and Merit), in two volumes, upper and lower, was [recorded] on the fourth day of the third month of the year of Water-Ox (the second year of the Yuan era), a Bingyin day. The monk-nun Daojian Hui, reflecting upon her own meager merit and lack of meritorious deeds, [recorded this].

I have humbly heard it said in the sutras that in cultivating fields of merit, one should not erect stupas or transcribe scriptures. Now, out of reverence for the Triple Gem, I have transcribed two fascicles of the *Jue zui fu jing* (Sutra on Resolving Sin and Merit), so as to serve as a cause for the future.

Furthermore, I vow that my teachers, elders, parents, and all those with whom I have karmic ties—whether they have already died or are yet to pass away—shall all receive deliverance and be led away from the three evil realms and the eight difficult conditions.
May they always encounter the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and resolve to attain Bodhicitta. I also vow that all sentient beings, like flowers in full bloom, shall universally share in this aspiration.
